summary: A 1970 set of notes from Steve Crocker on the protocol, following RFC 33. It updates RFC 33, and was in turn commented on and updated by RFC 39 and RFC 44. It is a working document from the early protocol design effort.

eli5.summary: These are the writer's extra thoughts on the rules for how computers should talk, adding to an earlier note.

questions: what are the arpanet host host control commands
how did early arpanet flow control work
what does the rsm command do
subtitle: Crocker's 1970 notes refining RFC 33: connection setup, flow control and a scheme for reconnection.

tldr.problem: The early network protocol needed flow control so a sender cannot flood a receiver, and a way to switch a connection from one socket to another.
tldr.mechanism: Connections are set up by exchanging RFC commands, flow is stopped by modifying RFNMs and restarted with RSM, and reconnection uses extra commands such as FND, END, RDY and ASG.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 33 and was updated by RFC 39 and RFC 44. The author says he lacks the experience to present reconnection in an integrated way.

today: RFC 36 is a working note with Unknown status. It updates RFC 33 and was updated by RFC 39 and RFC 44.

sections.title: Three Facilities
sections.content:
The protocol provides connection establishment, flow control and reconnection. Reconnection is treated separately partly because of its complexity and partly because the author does not have enough experience to present it in an integrated fashion.

Connection establishment works essentially as in RFC 33, with a more general form of switching provided independently of it. In the rough scenario, each process grabs a socket and requests a connection to the other, each NCP sends a Request-for-Connection (RFC) command, and the connection is established when each NCP has received an RFC and the RFNM for the one it sent. The sockets must be a send/receive pair.
sections.eli5: Two friends each pick a mailbox and tell the helpers to link them. They are connected once each helper has heard from the other.

sections.title: Flow Control
sections.content:
To stop a sender flooding a receiver, flow control is built into RFNM handling. A receiving host sends a special message to its IMP that modifies the next RFNM on a link. The sending host treats it as an RFNM and as a request to stop, and a confirming control command is returned. When the receiver is ready again it sends RSM to resume.

A footnote records that BB&N argues for unlimited buffering. The author bases the design on the assumption that only a small buffer exists at the receiving end.
sections.eli5: If you are being handed too many things, you can ask the sender to pause, then say "go on" when you have room.

sections.title: Data Structures
sections.content:
An NCP keeps five tables: a connection table, a process table, an input link table, an output link table and a link assignment table. The connection table is keyed by local socket and holds the foreign socket, link, connection state, flow state, a pointer to the user's process, reconnection state and a queue of waiting callers.

A local socket is a 32 bit number, a foreign socket is 40 bits, and a link is 8 bits. A socket is a receive socket if and only if its low-order bit is zero. Links are assigned by receivers.
sections.eli5: Each helper keeps lists to remember who is connected to whom and which roads are free.

sections.title: Control Commands
sections.content:
The command summary lists nine operation codes, from NOP (X'00') to ASG (X'08'). RFC starts a connection, CLS blocks, aborts or refuses one, RSM resumes a link and SPD acknowledges a stop.

Reconnection uses FND (Final End), END (End Found), RDY and ASG. FND chains through intermediate sockets and loop detection closes both sockets. END reports the socket at the end of a chain. RDY says all messages have been forwarded, and ASG assigns a new link to complete the reconnection.
sections.eli5: There is a short list of numbered signals. Some start or end a talk, some pause it, and some move it to a new mailbox.

references.text: Crocker, S., Carr, S., Cerf, V., "New HOST-HOST Protocol", RFC 33, February 1970.
